Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) troops filmed weapons they found after capturing Mekelle (Mekele), the capital of the Tigray Region, from the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF).
The weapons are being presented as TDF equipment, but that doesn't make much sense. Several of these weaponswould have required aircraft or heavy drones to deploy, making it more likely that this is an older weapons cache left behind by the ENDF, or a mixture of ENDF and TDF weapons.
Among the equipment visible are Chinese-made GB-25 laser-guided munitions, U.S.-made Mk 82 bombs, Russian-made FAB-500ShN bombs, R-60M/MK and R-73E air-to-air missiles, and what appears to be a dismantled Iranian-made Mohajer-6 unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV).

Why oil stays near $100 despite returning supply
The global oil market is caught between a fragile supply recovery and a rapidly dwindling safety cushion. Gulf producers have restored crude flows to near pre-war levels despite the continued disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, but the world's emergency stockpiles have been drained to levels Saudi Aramco's chief executive calls "scarily thin." The result is a market that looks calmer than at the height of the crisis but remains profoundly vulnerable to any new shock.
Amin Nasser, chief executive of Saudi Aramco, delivered a blunt assessment at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London: "Until Hormuz fully re-opens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify.” Even then, replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years, adding "2 million barrels per day of demand over the next 18 months" against global daily demand of just over 100 million barrels.
Nearly 3 billion barrels of oil supply have been lost since the conflict began, with more than 1 billion drawn from global stocks. Nasser estimated that fewer than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain, and most of that is "not practically available" — sitting in pipelines or representing the minimum volume needed to keep storage tanks operational. The planned release of up to 100 million barrels of emergency crude and diesel by G7 governments will buy time but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. "The system is already straining," he warned.
Meanwhile, the physical cost of moving oil has reached extraordinary levels. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have dwindled again as Iran intensifies attacks, eroding the brief success the US had in providing escorts for millions of barrels of crude. Iran has improved its targeting accuracy and stepped up attacks on ship-to-ship oil transfers. The daily charter rate for a very large crude carrier has surged past $1.3 million per day, compared with roughly $50,000 before the war began — an increase of more than 1,000%.
Gulf producers have adapted as best they can. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait have been using their own tankers to ship crude through Hormuz, and Aramco has restored flows on its East-West pipeline to about 80% of capacity. Nasser said Aramco is working on additional export routes to reduce dependence on any single corridor. But the recovery in volume has provided scant relief for prices: Brent crude has traded around $100 a barrel, roughly 40 percent higher than before the conflict began. As one analyst put it, a recovery in supply volume does not equal a full normalization of the supply system — the market is pricing not only how much crude is being loaded, but whether those barrels can be delivered safely, reliably, and at low cost.
The picture is of a market in precarious equilibrium. Supply is recovering, but the buffer that protects the world from further shocks has been largely exhausted. Shipping costs have become a structural burden rather than a temporary spike. Until Hormuz is fully reopened and confidence returns, Nasser's warning stands: the pressure at both ends of the barrel will only intensify. The system is already straining, and there is precious little left to absorb the next blow.
